title: HTML Attributes
summary: An HTML attribute gives an extra fact about a page part. It goes inside the start tag.
introduction: An HTML attribute gives an extra fact about a page part. It goes inside the start tag. A school bag might have a name label. An HTML element can have a label too. Add a link address, a class name and a language label.
learningObjectives: Write attributes with correct syntax and quoting
Use the global attributes id, class, title, lang, style and hidden appropriately
Recognise boolean attributes and data-* attributes

blocks.text: Attributes go inside the opening tag, separated by spaces, as `name="value"` pairs. Always quote the value with double quotes; it is the convention and it is required whenever the value contains spaces or special characters.

blocks.text: An unquoted value stops at the first space: `title=Visit the site` sets the title to `Visit` and then treats `the` and `site` as two bogus attributes. Quote every value.
Global attributes can be used on any element. These are the ones you will use most.

rows: A unique identifier for one element on the page. Used by links (`#id`), CSS and JavaScript.
One or more names, separated by spaces, shared by any number of elements. The main hook for CSS.
Advisory text, usually shown as a tooltip on hover.
The language of the element's content, for screen readers, spell checkers and search engines.
Inline CSS. Fine for quick tests, avoided in real projects in favour of stylesheets.

blocks.title: One id per page
blocks.text: An `id` must be unique in the document. Duplicate ids break fragment links, confuse `document.getElementById` and are invalid HTML. If several elements share a role, use a `class`.

Some attributes are on or off and need no value: `hidden`, `disabled`, `checked`, `required`, `readonly`, `autoplay`. Their presence means true. Writing `disabled="false"` does **not** turn the attribute off; the only way to switch it off is to remove it.

blocks.code:
<button disabled>Cannot click</button>
<button disabled="false">Still cannot click</button>
<button>Can click</button>

blocks.text: When you need to attach your own information to an element for JavaScript to read, use `data-*` attributes. They are valid HTML and show up in JavaScript as `element.dataset`.

Most attributes belong to particular elements: `href` on links, `src` and `alt` on images, `type` and `name` on inputs, `colspan` on table cells. The following lessons introduce them where they belong, and the [HTML reference](/references/html) lists them all in one place.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: If an attribute changes what the element *is* or *does* (`href`, `src`, `type`), it belongs in HTML. If it changes how the element *looks*, it belongs in CSS, not in a `style` attribute.
